claims.claim: Microglia in an individual developing CNS region during a specific time window are strikingly diverse.
claims.source: Cells from controls (Bax WT and Vehicle) were represented in every cluster (Figure 1), indicating that microglia in an individual developing CNS region during a specific time window are strikingly diverse.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that cells from controls were represented in every cluster.

claims.claim: Bax KO and PLX-treated microglia had dramatic and opposing shifts in their distribution compared to controls.
claims.source: Further, we found that Bax KO and PLX-treated microglia had dramatic and opposing shifts in their distribution compared to controls (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the UMAP plots in Figure 1C showing distribution of cells from each condition.

claims.claim: Cluster 0 is Apoe-enriched and has high expression of DAM, PAM, and ATM genes such as Lyz2 and Cd9, but also intermediate levels of homeostatic gene expression such as P2ry12 and Tmem119.
claims.source: While virtually every cell expressed Apoe and Ctsd, both genes were significantly enriched in cluster 0, which had high expression of other DAM (Keren-Shaul et al., 2017), PAM (Li et al., 2019a), and ATM (Hammond et al., 2019) genes, such as Lyz2 and Cd9, but also intermediate levels of homeostatic gene expression such as P2ry12 and Tmem119.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the gene expression data shown in Figure 1D and Supplementary file 1.

claims.claim: Cluster 1 is the Homeostatic cluster with highest expression of Tmem119 and P2ry12 as well as other homeostatic genes.
claims.source: Cluster 1 had highest expression of Tmem119 and P2ry12 as well as other homeostatic genes, including Itgam, Siglech, Tgfbr1, P2ry13, Selplg, and Adgrg1 and so we named it Homeostatic.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the gene expression data shown in Figure 1D and Supplementary file 1.

claims.claim: Cluster 2 is the Hom/chemokine cluster enriched for chemokines including Ccl4 and Ccl3 and has intermediate/high expression of homeostatic genes.
claims.source: Cluster 2 was enriched for chemokines including Ccl4 and Ccl3, two genes previously found in injury-responsive microglia in demyelinated lesions (Hammond et al., 2019) and in PAM of developing WM tracts (Li et al., 2019a), and had intermediate/high expression of homeostatic genes (e.g. Tmem119; Figure 1) and so we termed it Hom/chemokine cluster.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the gene expression data shown in Figure 1D and Supplementary file 1.

claims.claim: Ccl3 and Ccl4 were previously found in injury-responsive microglia in demyelinated lesions.
claims.source: Cluster 2 was enriched for chemokines including Ccl4 and Ccl3, two genes previously found in injury-responsive microglia in demyelinated lesions (Hammond et al., 2019) and in PAM of developing WM tracts (Li et al., 2019a), and had intermediate/high expression of homeostatic genes (e.g. Tmem119; Figure 1) and so we termed it Hom/chemokine cluster.
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hammond et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Ccl3 and Ccl4 were previously found in PAM of developing WM tracts.
claims.source: Cluster 2 was enriched for chemokines including Ccl4 and Ccl3, two genes previously found in injury-responsive microglia in demyelinated lesions (Hammond et al., 2019) and in PAM of developing WM tracts (Li et al., 2019a), and had intermediate/high expression of homeostatic genes (e.g. Tmem119; Figure 1) and so we termed it Hom/chemokine cluster.
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Li et al., 2019a.

claims.claim: Retinal microglia express Ccl3 and Ccl4 in vivo.
claims.source: Ccl3 and Ccl4 are among a set of genes that can be induced by dissociation (Marsh et al., 2020) so we confirmed that retinal microglia express Ccl3 and Ccl4 in vivo by in situ hybridization (Figure 1—figure supplement 5 and data not shown).
claims.evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claims.claim: Cluster 3 is the PLX-enriched cluster marked by Npl and Apoc1 and was substantially increased in PLX-treated retinas.
claims.source: Cluster 3 was marked by Npl, found in lipid-droplet microglia (Marschallinger et al., 2020), and Apoc1, a lipoprotein high in multiple sclerosis-associated human microglia (Masuda et al., 2019). Since this cluster was substantially increased in PLX-treated retinas, we named this cluster PLX-enriched.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the gene expression data shown in Figure 1D and the cluster distribution data in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: Npl is found in lipid-droplet microglia.
claims.source: Cluster 3 was marked by Npl, found in lipid-droplet microglia (Marschallinger et al., 2020), and Apoc1, a lipoprotein high in multiple sclerosis-associated human microglia (Masuda et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Marschallinger et al., 2020.

claims.claim: Apoc1 is a lipoprotein high in multiple sclerosis-associated human microglia.
claims.source: Cluster 3 was marked by Npl, found in lipid-droplet microglia (Marschallinger et al., 2020), and Apoc1, a lipoprotein high in multiple sclerosis-associated human microglia (Masuda et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Masuda et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Cluster 4 is the Chemokine/cytokine cluster with high expression of chemokines Cxcl2 and Cxcl10 and pro-inflammatory cytokines such as Il1b and Tnf.
claims.source: Chemokines Cxcl2 and Cxcl10 and pro-inflammatory cytokines, such as Il1b and Tnf, were high in Cluster 4, dubbed the Chemokine/cytokine cluster.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the gene expression data shown in Figure 1D and Supplementary file 1.

claims.claim: Cluster 5 is the ATM/PAM-like cluster with specific expression of Spp1 and high expression of Fabp5, Ctsl, Lpl, Igf1, and Csf1.
claims.source: Cluster 5 most resembled ATM (Hammond et al., 2019) (69/193 genes shared) and PAM (Li et al., 2019a) (79/193 genes shared) with specific expression of Spp1 and high expression of Fabp5, Ctsl, Lpl, Igf1, and Csf1 and thus we termed it ATM/PAM-like.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the gene expression data shown in Figure 1D and Supplementary file 1, and comparison to published datasets.

claims.claim: Cluster 5 shares 69/193 genes with ATM.
claims.source: Cluster 5 most resembled ATM (Hammond et al., 2019) (69/193 genes shared) and PAM (Li et al., 2019a) (79/193 genes shared) with specific expression of Spp1 and high expression of Fabp5, Ctsl, Lpl, Igf1, and Csf1 and thus we termed it ATM/PAM-like.
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparison to the ATM dataset from Hammond et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Cluster 5 shares 79/193 genes with PAM.
claims.source: Cluster 5 most resembled ATM (Hammond et al., 2019) (69/193 genes shared) and PAM (Li et al., 2019a) (79/193 genes shared) with specific expression of Spp1 and high expression of Fabp5, Ctsl, Lpl, Igf1, and Csf1 and thus we termed it ATM/PAM-like.
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparison to the PAM dataset from Li et al., 2019a.

claims.claim: Cluster 6 is the Antioxidant-responsive cluster with high expression of antioxidant responsive genes Hmox1 and Gclm.
claims.source: Cluster 6 was named Antioxidant-responsive cluster due to high expression of antioxidant responsive genes, Hmox1 and Gclm (Rojo et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the gene expression data shown in Figure 1D and Supplementary file 1.

claims.claim: Clusters 7, 8, and 9 represent Cycling microglia and expressed Mki67, Top2a, and Mcm genes.
claims.source: Clusters 7, 8, and 9 represented Cycling microglia and expressed Mki67, Top2a, and Mcm genes.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the gene expression data shown in Figure 1D and Supplementary file 1.

claims.claim: Cluster 10 is the Interferon-responsive cluster with high and very specific expression of interferon response genes such as Ccl5, Ifit3, and Ifitm3.
claims.source: Cluster 10, the smallest, contained 71 cells with high and very specific expression of interferon response genes such as Ccl5, Ifit3, and Ifitm3 (Dorman et al., 2022) and was thus termed Interferon-responsive cluster.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the gene expression data shown in Figure 1D and Supplementary file 1.

claims.claim: There is a continuum of expression of homeostatic genes Tmem119 and P2ry12 across the clusters that appears to be inverse to broadly expressed DAM/PAM/ATM genes such as Apoe and Ctsd.
claims.source: We noted a continuum of expression of the homeostatic genes Tmem119 and P2ry12 across the clusters that appeared to be inverse to broadly expressed DAM/PAM/ATM genes such as Apoe and Ctsd (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the gene expression data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 2C.

claims.claim: There is a gradient of expression of homeostatic genes including Siglech, Tgfbr1, and Selplg which were highest in Homeostatic cluster (1), high/intermediate in Hom/chemokine (2), intermediate in Apoe-enriched (0), Chemokine/cytokine cluster (4), ATM/PAM-like (5), Antioxidant-responsive (6), and Interferon-responsive (10), with lowest expression in PLX-enriched cluster (3).
claims.source: As for Tmem119 and P2ry12, we found a gradient of expression of homeostatic genes including Siglech, Tgfbr1, and Selplg which were highest in Homeostatic cluster (1), high/intermediate in Hom/chemokine (2), intermediate in Apoe-enriched (0), Chemokine/cytokine cluster (4), ATM/PAM-like (5), Antioxidant-responsive (6), and Interferon-responsive (10), with lowest expression in PLX-enriched cluster (3), suggesting a spectrum from more to less homeostatic (Figure 2C and C').
claims.evidence: This is supported by the gene expression data shown in Figure 2C and C'.

claims.claim: The gradient of homeostatic gene expression suggests a spectrum from more to less homeostatic microglia.
claims.source: As for Tmem119 and P2ry12, we found a gradient of expression of homeostatic genes including Siglech, Tgfbr1, and Selplg which were highest in Homeostatic cluster (1), high/intermediate in Hom/chemokine (2), intermediate in Apoe-enriched (0), Chemokine/cytokine cluster (4), ATM/PAM-like (5), Antioxidant-responsive (6), and Interferon-responsive (10), with lowest expression in PLX-enriched cluster (3), suggesting a spectrum from more to less homeostatic (Figure 2C and C').
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observed gradient of homeostatic gene expression.

claims.claim: Lysosomal genes including Lyz2, Galns and Cst7 were either low, absent, or sparse in Homeostatic cluster (1) and Hom/chemokine (2) and generally more highly or broadly expressed in Apoe-enriched (0), PLX-enriched (3), Chemokine/cytokine cluster (4), ATM/PAM-like (5), Antioxidant-responsive (6), and Interferon-responsive (10).
claims.source: To determine whether this related to shifting phagocytic function of microglia, we examined the expression of lysosomal genes including Lyz2, Galns and Cst7 and saw roughly the opposite pattern. These genes were either low, absent, or sparse in Homeostatic cluster (1) and Hom/chemokine (2) and generally more highly or broadly expressed in Apoe-enriched (0), PLX-enriched (3), Chemokine/cytokine cluster (4), ATM/PAM-like (5), Antioxidant-responsive (6), and Interferon-responsive (10) (Figure 2D and D').
claims.evidence: This is supported by the gene expression data shown in Figure 2D and D'.

claims.claim: Cluster 3 had the greatest enrichment of Lysosomal genes (35/552), followed by clusters 5, 10, 6, 4, and 0, with homeostatic clusters (1 and 2) expressing the lowest number of genes.
claims.source: Comparing our clusters to a gene ontology (GO) list of 552 Lysosomal genes (GO:0005764) (Bult et al., 2019), we found cluster 3 had the greatest enrichment (35/552), followed by clusters 5, 10, 6, 4, and 0, with homeostatic clusters (1 and 2) expressing the lowest number of genes.
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparison of cluster gene expression to the GO list of Lysosomal genes.

claims.claim: Genes involved in lipid metabolism and cholesterol transport followed the same trend as lysosomal genes across clusters.
claims.source: Additionally, genes involved in lipid metabolism and cholesterol transport, important processes following the engulfment of apoptotic cells (Doran et al., 2020), followed the same trend (Figure 2E and E').
claims.evidence: This is supported by the gene expression data shown in Figure 2E and E'.

claims.claim: Cluster 3 expressed the highest number (36/1428) of Lipid Metabolic process genes (GO:0006629), followed by 5, 6, 4, and 10 while homeostatic clusters (1 and 2) expressed the lowest number.
claims.source: Cluster 3 again expressed the highest number (36/1428) of Lipid Metabolic process genes (GO:0006629) (Bult et al., 2019), followed by 5, 6, 4, and 10 while homeostatic clusters (1 and 2) expressed the lowest number.
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparison of cluster gene expression to the GO list of Lipid Metabolic process genes.

claims.claim: Microglia in clusters (0,3,4,5,6,10) are equipped to be actively breaking down phagocytosed material compared to more homeostatic clusters (1,2).
claims.source: Thus, microglia in clusters (0,3,4,5,6,10) are equipped to be actively breaking down phagocytosed material compared to more homeostatic clusters (1,2).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the high expression of lysosomal and lipid metabolism genes in these clusters.

claims.claim: Clusters 0,3,4,5,6, and 10 are involved in active remodeling activities and are referred to as remodeling clusters.
claims.source: Therefore, we hypothesize that clusters 0,3,4,5,6, and 10 are involved in active remodeling activities and refer to them as remodeling clusters (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the gene expression patterns observed in these clusters.

claims.claim: Genes involved in lysosomal and lipid metabolism function were enriched in remodeling clusters by differential expression analysis on clusters (1,2) compared to (0,3,4,5,6,10).
claims.source: We confirmed genes involved in lysosomal and lipid metabolism function were enriched in remodeling clusters by differential expression analysis on clusters (1,2) compared to (0,3,4,5,6,10) (Supplementary file 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by differential expression analysis data in Supplementary file 2.

claims.claim: DAM/ATM/PAM-related genes such as Igf1, Itgax, and Axl had similar low expression in Homeostatic cluster (1) and Hom/chemokine (2) and higher expression in the remodeling clusters (0,3,4,5,6,10).
claims.source: We next examined the expression of additional DAM/ATM/PAM-related genes, including Igf1, and recognition receptors Itgax and Axl. We noted similar low expression in Homeostatic cluster (1) and Hom/chemokine (2) and higher expression in the remodeling clusters (0,3,4,5,6,10) (Figure 2F and F').
claims.evidence: This is supported by the gene expression data shown in Figure 2F and F'.

claims.claim: DAM/PAM/ATM-related genes had varying cluster specificity, with genes such as Apoe expressed in nearly every cell, whereas Igf1 and Spp1 were more restricted to specific clusters.
claims.source: Interestingly, DAM/PAM/ATM-related genes had varying cluster specificity. Genes such as Apoe were expressed in nearly every cell (Figure 1), whereas Igf1 and Spp1 were more restricted to specific clusters, suggesting that regulation of these genes is complex (Figure 2F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the gene expression data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 2F.

claims.claim: Regulation of DAM/PAM/ATM-related genes is complex.
claims.source: Interestingly, DAM/PAM/ATM-related genes had varying cluster specificity. Genes such as Apoe were expressed in nearly every cell (Figure 1), whereas Igf1 and Spp1 were more restricted to specific clusters, suggesting that regulation of these genes is complex (Figure 2F).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the varying cluster specificity of DAM/PAM/ATM-related genes.

claims.claim: Phagolysosomal function defines the spectrum of microglial states in the postnatal retina.
claims.source: Together, these results suggest that phagolysosomal function defines the spectrum of microglial states in the postnatal retina.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the observed gradient of lysosomal and lipid metabolism gene expression across clusters.

claims.claim: There was a dramatic shift in cluster distribution with the loss of Bax compared to littermate controls.
claims.source: We examined microglia from Bax KO retinas in which apoptotic death programs in RGCs and other neurons are selectively lost (Fricker et al., 2018) and saw a dramatic shift in cluster distribution with the loss of Bax compared to littermate controls (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the UMAP plots and cluster distribution data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claims.claim: There was a fivefold expansion in the Homeostatic cluster (1) in Bax KO compared to WT.
claims.source: We found a fivefold expansion in the Homeostatic cluster (1) in Bax KO compared to WT (Figure 3A, B and C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the cluster distribution data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: Remodeling clusters Apoe-enriched (0), Chemokine/cytokine expressing (4), ATM/PAM-like (5), and PLX-enriched (3) were 4.7-fold, 3.46-fold, 5.86-fold, and fivefold more abundant in WT compared to Bax KO, respectively.
claims.source: This was concurrent with decreases in remodeling clusters Apoe-enriched (0), Chemokine/cytokine expressing (4), and ATM/PAM-like (5), and the minor PLX-enriched cluster (3), which were 4.7-fold, 3.46-fold, 5.86-fold, and fivefold more abundant in WT, respectively (Figure 3A and B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the cluster distribution data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: Clusters Hom/chemokine (2), Antioxidant-responsive (6), Cycling (7–9), and Interferon-responsive (10) remained largely unaltered in Bax KO compared to WT.
claims.source: Clusters that remained largely unaltered included Hom/chemokine (2), Antioxidant-responsive (6), Cycling (7–9), and Interferon-responsive (10), suggesting they were not driven by apoptotic cell interactions or clearance (Figure 3A and B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the cluster distribution data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: Clusters Hom/chemokine (2), Antioxidant-responsive (6), Cycling (7–9), and Interferon-responsive (10) were not driven by apoptotic cell interactions or clearance.
claims.source: Clusters that remained largely unaltered included Hom/chemokine (2), Antioxidant-responsive (6), Cycling (7–9), and Interferon-responsive (10), suggesting they were not driven by apoptotic cell interactions or clearance (Figure 3A and B).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that these clusters remained largely unaltered in Bax KO.

claims.claim: The spectrum of homeostatic to more remodeling clusters (0,3,4, and 5) in the postnatal retina is driven predominately by neuronal apoptosis.
claims.source: Therefore, we conclude that the spectrum of homeostatic to more remodeling clusters (0,3,4, and 5) in the postnatal retina is driven predominately by neuronal apoptosis.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observed changes in cluster distribution in Bax KO compared to WT.

claims.claim: Tmem119, P2ry12, and Siglech were among the 133 upregulated genes in microglia from Bax KO retina.
claims.source: Consistent with a shift to a more homeostatic state, Tmem119, P2ry12, and Siglech were among the 133 upregulated genes in microglia from Bax KO retina.
claims.evidence: This is supported by differential expression analysis data shown in Figure 3D and Supplementary file 3.

claims.claim: The 183 downregulated genes in Bax KO microglia included lysosomal and lipid metabolism genes such as Apoe, Lyz2, Cst7, Ctsb, Lpl and Cd68, DAM/PAM/ATM-related genes such as Igf1 and Spp1, and recognition receptors Itgax and Axl.
claims.source: The 183 downregulated genes included lysosomal and lipid metabolism genes such as Apoe, Lyz2, Cst7, Ctsb, Lpl and Cd68, DAM/PAM/ATM-related genes such as Igf1 and Spp1, and recognition receptors Itgax and Axl (Figure 3C and D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by differential expression analysis data shown in Figure 3D and Supplementary file 3.

claims.claim: KEGG analysis on downregulated genes in Bax KO identified metabolic and lysosomal pathways as significantly reduced.
claims.source: We next performed KEGG analysis using GeneCodis 4 (García-Moreno et al., 2021) on downregulated genes in Bax KO to identify major pathways driven by interactions with dying neurons (Figure 3E). Consistent with the idea that microglial phagocytosis was a key factor in these gene expression changes, we found metabolic and lysosomal pathways significantly reduced.
claims.evidence: This is supported by KEGG pathway analysis data shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: Microglial phagocytosis is a key factor in gene expression changes driven by interactions with dying neurons.
claims.source: We next performed KEGG analysis using GeneCodis 4 (García-Moreno et al., 2021) on downregulated genes in Bax KO to identify major pathways driven by interactions with dying neurons (Figure 3E). Consistent with the idea that microglial phagocytosis was a key factor in these gene expression changes, we found metabolic and lysosomal pathways significantly reduced.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the KEGG pathway analysis showing reduced metabolic and lysosomal pathways in Bax KO.

claims.claim: Microglia remained uniformly spaced in Bax KO retinas.
claims.source: To determine whether loss of Bax altered microglia density or distribution, we used C1q as a marker for microglia, which we validated by both scRNAseq (Figure 1—figure supplement 4C) and immunostaining (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B). We found that microglia remained uniformly spaced but that density was reduced by nearly half in Bax KO retinas (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D), consistent with our prior flow cytometry analysis (Anderson et al., 2019a).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: Microglial density was reduced by nearly half in Bax KO retinas.
claims.source: To determine whether loss of Bax altered microglia density or distribution, we used C1q as a marker for microglia, which we validated by both scRNAseq (Figure 1—figure supplement 4C) and immunostaining (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B). We found that microglia remained uniformly spaced but that density was reduced by nearly half in Bax KO retinas (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D), consistent with our prior flow cytometry analysis (Anderson et al., 2019a).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D and citation to Anderson et al., 2019a.

claims.claim: Neuronal apoptosis is important for regulating microglial density.
claims.source: Altogether, this suggests that neuronal apoptosis regulates important properties of microglia in the postnatal retina, including overall density as well as the emergence of multiple remodeling states.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observed reduction in microglial density in Bax KO retinas.

claims.claim: Neuronal apoptosis regulates the emergence of multiple remodeling states in microglia.
claims.source: Altogether, this suggests that neuronal apoptosis regulates important properties of microglia in the postnatal retina, including overall density as well as the emergence of multiple remodeling states.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observed changes in cluster distribution in Bax KO retinas.

claims.claim: ~60% of microglia in postnatal retina survive inhibition of CSF1R signaling.
claims.source: A striking property of microglia in postnatal retina is that ~60% survive inhibition of CSF1R signaling, while only very small subsets show this property in postnatal brain (Anderson et al., 2019a) or adult brain (Zhan et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Anderson et al., 2019a and Zhan et al., 2020.

claims.claim: Only very small subsets of microglia survive CSF1R inhibition in postnatal brain.
claims.source: A striking property of microglia in postnatal retina is that ~60% survive inhibition of CSF1R signaling, while only very small subsets show this property in postnatal brain (Anderson et al., 2019a) or adult brain (Zhan et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Anderson et al., 2019a.

claims.claim: Only very small subsets of microglia survive CSF1R inhibition in adult brain.
claims.source: A striking property of microglia in postnatal retina is that ~60% survive inhibition of CSF1R signaling, while only very small subsets show this property in postnatal brain (Anderson et al., 2019a) or adult brain (Zhan et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zhan et al., 2020.

claims.claim: Surviving microglia following CSF1R inhibition had reduced homeostatic gene expression and increased DAM/PAM/ATM gene expression, and this required neuronal apoptosis.
claims.source: We previously found that surviving microglia had reduced homeostatic gene expression and increased DAM/PAM/ATM gene expression, and this required neuronal apoptosis (Anderson et al., 2019a).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work, Anderson et al., 2019a.

claims.claim: There was a large shift in the distribution of cells across clusters with PLX treatment.
claims.source: We examined scRNAseq of Vehicle and PLX-treated microglia (dosed for 3 days) and found a large shift in the distribution of cells across clusters with PLX treatment (Figure 4A and B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the UMAP plots and cluster distribution data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claims.claim: Several remodeling clusters were either enriched or maintained following PLX treatment.
claims.source: Several remodeling clusters were either enriched or maintained.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the cluster distribution data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: PLX-enriched cluster (3) represented nearly 60% of remaining microglia following PLX3397 (increased sixtyfold).
claims.source: The least homeostatic cluster, PLX-enriched (3), which was a very small proportion of cells in both Vehicle and Bax WT (Figure 3A and B), represented nearly 60% of remaining microglia following PLX3397 (increased sixtyfold) and thus seemed to arise, in part, by treatment (Figure 4A and B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the cluster distribution data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: PLX-enriched cluster (3) seemed to arise, in part, by PLX3397 treatment.
claims.source: The least homeostatic cluster, PLX-enriched (3), which was a very small proportion of cells in both Vehicle and Bax WT (Figure 3A and B), represented nearly 60% of remaining microglia following PLX3397 (increased sixtyfold) and thus seemed to arise, in part, by treatment (Figure 4A and B).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the dramatic increase in this cluster following PLX treatment.

claims.claim: The expansion of PLX-enriched (3) microglia could potentially be due to the further reduction of homeostatic properties of surviving microglia with CSF1R blockade.
claims.source: This could potentially be due to the further reduction of homeostatic properties of surviving microglia with CSF1R blockade (Kempthorne et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is a speculation supported by a citation to Kempthorne et al., 2020.

claims.claim: Remodeling cluster Chemokine/cytokine (4) was increased twofold with PLX-treatment.
claims.source: Remodeling cluster Chemokine/cytokine (4) was increased twofold with PLX-treatment and ATM/PAM-like (5), Antioxidant-responsive (6), and Interferon-responsive (10) were slightly reduced or unchanged (0.755-fold, 0.654-fold, 0.979-fold, respectively), suggesting they are more resistant than other subsets (Figure 4A and B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the cluster distribution data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: ATM/PAM-like (5), Antioxidant-responsive (6), and Interferon-responsive (10) clusters were slightly reduced or unchanged with PLX-treatment (0.755-fold, 0.654-fold, 0.979-fold, respectively), suggesting they are more resistant than other subsets.
claims.source: Remodeling cluster Chemokine/cytokine (4) was increased twofold with PLX-treatment and ATM/PAM-like (5), Antioxidant-responsive (6), and Interferon-responsive (10) were slightly reduced or unchanged (0.755-fold, 0.654-fold, 0.979-fold, respectively), suggesting they are more resistant than other subsets (Figure 4A and B).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the cluster distribution data showing these clusters were maintained or slightly reduced following PLX treatment.

claims.claim: Clusters with high or intermediate expression of homeostatic genes, Apoe-enriched (0), Homeostatic (1), Hom/chemokine (2), and Cycling (7,8,9) were largely absent following PLX treatment.
claims.source: Conversely, we found clusters that had high or intermediate expression of homeostatic genes, Apoe-enriched (0), Homeostatic (1), Hom/chemokine (2), and Cycling (7,8,9) were largely absent following PLX treatment, suggesting these clusters are more dependent on CSF1R for survival or that they had shifted to a different state (Figure 4A and B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the cluster distribution data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: Clusters Apoe-enriched (0), Homeostatic (1), Hom/chemokine (2), and Cycling (7,8,9) are more dependent on CSF1R for survival or they had shifted to a different state.
claims.source: Conversely, we found clusters that had high or intermediate expression of homeostatic genes, Apoe-enriched (0), Homeostatic (1), Hom/chemokine (2), and Cycling (7,8,9) were largely absent following PLX treatment, suggesting these clusters are more dependent on CSF1R for survival or that they had shifted to a different state (Figure 4A and B).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that these clusters were largely absent following PLX treatment.

claims.claim: There is overlap between clusters dependent on neuronal apoptosis (0,3,4, and 5) and resistant to loss of CSF1R signaling (3,4,5,6, and 10).
claims.source: We noted the overlap between clusters dependent on neuronal apoptosis (0,3,4, and 5) and resistant to loss of CSF1R signaling (3,4,5,6, and 10), illustrating the link between the two and arguing that certain microglial states driven by neuronal apoptosis may confer resistance to CSF1R inhibition.
claims.evidence: This is an observation based on comparing the cluster distribution data from Bax KO and PLX-treated samples.

claims.claim: Certain microglial states driven by neuronal apoptosis may confer resistance to CSF1R inhibition.
claims.source: We noted the overlap between clusters dependent on neuronal apoptosis (0,3,4, and 5) and resistant to loss of CSF1R signaling (3,4,5,6, and 10), illustrating the link between the two and arguing that certain microglial states driven by neuronal apoptosis may confer resistance to CSF1R inhibition.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observed overlap between clusters dependent on neuronal apoptosis and resistant to CSF1R inhibition.

claims.claim: Downregulation of Csf1r alone does not alter dependence on CSF1R signaling.

claims.claim: Microglia maturation may not be a key factor in CSF1R dependence in the context of development.

claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the authors' previous findings, supported by citations to Anderson et al., 2019b and Anderson et al., 2019a.

claims.claim: Most PLX-resistant microglia subsets are induced by neuronal apoptosis.
claims.source: We find that most of these resistant microglia subsets are induced by neuronal apoptosis, consistent with our prior analysis showing increased microglial dependence on CSF1R in Bax KO retina (Anderson et al., 2019a).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observed overlap between clusters dependent on neuronal apoptosis and resistant to CSF1R inhibition, supported by a citation to Anderson et al., 2019a.

claims.claim: Peritoneal and bone marrow macrophages that phagocytose apoptotic cells survive in the absence of serum or survival factors in culture.
claims.source: Interestingly, in culture, peritoneal and bone marrow macrophages that phagocytose apoptotic cells also survive in the absence of serum or survival factors (Reddy et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Reddy et al., 2002.

claims.claim: In periods of elevated cell death and possible lack of extrinsic survival factors, phagocytes such as microglia might have evolved strategies to survive in order to maintain homeostasis or reduce inflammation.
claims.source: In periods of elevated cell death and possible lack of extrinsic survival factors, such as neuronally expressed CSF1R ligand, IL-34 (Nandi et al., 2012), phagocytes such as microglia might have evolved strategies to survive in order to maintain homeostasis or reduce inflammation (Reddy et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed survival of phagocytes in the absence of survival factors, supported by citations to Nandi et al., 2012 and Reddy et al., 2002.

claims.claim: Cholesterol, along with CSF-1/IL-34 and TGF-ß2, has been shown to be an important survival factor for microglia in culture.
claims.source: Importantly, cholesterol, along with CSF-1/IL-34 and TGF-ß2, has been shown to be an important survival factor for microglia in culture (Bohlen et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bohlen et al., 2017.

claims.claim: PLX-treatment itself could be inducing transcriptional changes reminiscent of remodeling states.
claims.source: However, other possibilities exist for the overlap between clusters dependent on neuronal apoptosis (0,3,4,5) and clusters more resistant to CSF1R inhibition (3,4,5,6,10). For example, PLX-treatment itself could be inducing transcriptional changes reminiscent of remodeling states.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation about alternative explanations for the observed overlap.

claims.claim: CSF1R signaling may be important for promoting microglial homeostasis.
claims.source: Thus, CSF1R signaling may also be important for promoting microglial homeostasis (Hu et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hu et al., 2021.

claims.claim: Mutations in CSF1R can lead to leukoencephalopathy, a neurodegenerative disorder that is associated with loss of homeostatic microglia phenotype.
claims.source: Consistent with this, mutations in CSF1R can lead to leukoencephalopathy, a neurodegenerative disorder that is associated with loss of homeostatic microglia phenotype (Kempthorne et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kempthorne et al., 2020.

claims.claim: PLX-enriched (3) microglia may represent cells that are undergoing other changes, even progressing toward death.
claims.source: PLX-enriched (3) microglia may also represent cells that are undergoing other changes, even progressing toward death.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation about the nature of PLX-enriched microglia.

claims.claim: Axl has been shown to inhibit apoptosis in a variety of cell types including fibroblasts, oligodendrocytes, and Gonadotropin-releasing hormone neurons in the brain.
claims.source: Axl has been shown to inhibit apoptosis in a variety of cell types (Axelrod and Pienta, 2014) including fibroblasts (Goruppi et al., 1997), oligodendrocytes in contexts of growth factor withdrawal or TNF toxicity (Shankar et al., 2006), and in Gonadotropin-releasing hormone neurons in the brain (Pierce et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Axelrod and Pienta, 2014; Goruppi et al., 1997; Shankar et al., 2006; Pierce et al., 2008.

claims.claim: Axl's role in various types of cancer has been well established for promoting tumor growth and metastasis in part due to its ability to inhibit apoptosis of cancer cells.
claims.source: Its role in various types of cancer has been well established for promoting tumor growth and metastasis in part due to its ability to inhibit apoptosis of cancer cells (Zhu et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zhu et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Axl has diverse downstream signaling cascades depending on context.
claims.source: Axl has diverse downstream signaling cascades depending on context (Axelrod and Pienta, 2014), but one candidate signaling cascade is the PI3K-Akt-NfkB-Bcl2 pathway.
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Axelrod and Pienta, 2014.

claims.claim: Activation of PI3K and Akt has shown to be important for survival of cultured macrophages, oligodendrocytes, neurons, and cancer cells.
claims.source: Activation of PI3K and Akt has shown to be important for survival of cultured macrophages (Reddy et al., 2002), oligodendrocytes (Shankar et al., 2003; Shankar et al., 2006), neurons (Pierce et al., 2008) as well as cancer cells (Axelrod and Pienta, 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Reddy et al., 2002; Shankar et al., 2003; Shankar et al., 2006; Pierce et al., 2008; Axelrod and Pienta, 2014.

claims.claim: Spp1/osteopontin is a candidate pathway for regulating microglial survival since it was significantly downregulated in Axl KO microglia.
claims.source: Another candidate pathway for regulating microglial survival is Spp1/osteopontin since we found it was significantly downregulated in Axl KO microglia.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the bulk RNA-seq data showing Spp1 was downregulated in Axl KO microglia.

claims.claim: Spp1/osteopontin has been shown to promote survival of other cell types including peripheral immune cells and cancer cells.
claims.source: Spp1/osteopontin has been shown to promote survival of other cell types including peripheral immune cells (Denhardt et al., 2001) and cancer cells (Saleh et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Denhardt et al., 2001 and Saleh et al., 2016.

claims.source: Furthermore, Spp1/osteopontin can influence aspects of microglial properties including enhancing survival under conditions of stress in culture (Yu et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Yu et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Neuronal cell death is a key factor driving multiple states of microglia in developing retina, with distinct transcriptional profiles and altered dependence from CSF1R signaling for survival.
claims.source: Altogether, we show neuronal cell death is a key factor driving multiple states of microglia in developing retina, with distinct transcriptional profiles and altered dependence from CSF1R signaling for survival.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion integrating multiple experimental findings from the study.

claims.claim: Apoptotic cell recognition by microglia is a critical developmental event driving diverse effects on gene expression, clearance, and survival, with distinct pathways involved in mediating each of these responses.
claims.source: Apoptotic cell recognition by microglia is thus a critical developmental event driving diverse effects on gene expression, clearance, and survival, with distinct pathways involved in mediating each of these responses.

results.result: Single-cell RNA sequencing of postnatal retinal microglia reveals 11 distinct clusters with varying gene expression profiles, including homeostatic, remodeling, cycling, and interferon-responsive states.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C71 describe the identification and characterization of 11 microglial clusters using scRNAseq. The data in Figure 1 and Supplementary file 1 provide clear evidence for distinct clusters with specific marker genes. The clustering is well-supported by UMAP visualization and differential gene expression analysis.

results.result: Postnatal retinal microglia exist on a spectrum from homeostatic to remodeling states, defined by inverse gradients of homeostatic genes (Tmem119, P2ry12) and lysosomal/lipid metabolism genes, with phagolysosomal function defining this spectrum.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C85 describe gene expression gradients across clusters shown in Figure 2. The data demonstrate clear inverse relationships between homeostatic and remodeling gene expression, supported by GO term enrichment analysis. The conclusion that phagolysosomal function defines the spectrum is well-supported by the systematic analysis of lysosomal and lipid metabolism genes.

results.result: Neuronal apoptosis drives multiple microglial remodeling states, as demonstrated by dramatic shifts in cluster distribution in Bax KO mice, with a fivefold expansion of homeostatic microglia and corresponding decreases in remodeling clusters.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C45, C86-C99 describe the Bax KO experiment shown in Figure 3. The data clearly demonstrate that loss of neuronal apoptosis shifts microglia toward homeostatic states, with robust quantification of cluster distribution changes, differential gene expression, and KEGG pathway analysis. The reduction in microglial density in Bax KO is also well-documented.

results.result: Several microglial remodeling states driven by neuronal apoptosis are resistant to CSF1R inhibition, while homeostatic microglia are more dependent on CSF1R signaling for survival, with resistance linked to increased phagocytosis and lysosomal function.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C46, C104-C121 describe the PLX3397 treatment experiment shown in Figure 4. The data demonstrate clear shifts in cluster distribution with PLX treatment, with remodeling clusters maintained or enriched while homeostatic clusters are depleted. The overlap between apoptosis-dependent and PLX-resistant clusters is well-documented, though the causal relationship requires careful interpretation.

results.result: CR3 and Mer receptors are required for timely clearance of apoptotic RGCs during postnatal development, while CX3CR1 and Axl are dispensable for this process.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C122-C128 describe the receptor knockout experiments shown in Figure 5. The immunostaining data clearly demonstrate increased dying RGCs (CC3+RBPMS+) in CR3 KO and Mertk KO retinas, with appropriate controls showing no change in overall RGC density or vascular development. The statistical analysis supports the conclusions.

results.result: Axl, but not CR3, CX3CR1, or Mer, is consequential for microglial survival in the absence of CSF1R signaling, with Axl being induced by neuronal apoptosis.
results.evaluation: Claims C10, C129-C135 describe the PLX3397 treatment of receptor knockout mice shown in Figure 6. The flow cytometry data clearly demonstrate that only Axl KO shows increased microglial depletion following PLX treatment, matching Bax KO levels. The induction of Axl by neuronal apoptosis is supported by the differential expression data from Figure 3D.

results.result: Loss of Mer, Axl, or both does not have widespread impact on expression of microglial remodeling genes, suggesting that TAM receptor-mediated signaling or reduced clearance are not sufficient to drive remodeling gene expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C9, C47-C50, C136-C148 describe the bulk RNA-seq experiments shown in Figure 7. The data demonstrate modest changes in gene expression in Mertk KO, Axl KO, and Mertk/Axl dKO microglia, with minimal effects on lysosomal, lipid metabolism, or DAM/PAM/ATM-related genes. This is a negative result but well-supported by the data.

results.result: Microglia serve critical remodeling roles in the developing nervous system, responding to environmental changes with phagocytosis or soluble factor secretion.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C12-C15 are general statements about microglial function supported by established knowledge and citations. These provide appropriate context for the study but are not novel findings.

results.result: Recent scRNAseq studies have revealed microglial diversity during development, but the cues promoting this diversity are not well defined, representing a central challenge in the field.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C3, C16-C18 describe the current state of knowledge and motivation for the study, supported by citations. These establish the knowledge gap but are not experimental findings.

results.result: Apoptotic cell death is fundamental for organ development, including the CNS, with efferocytosis by microglia being important for maintaining homeostasis. The postnatal retina is an excellent model system where ~50% of RGCs undergo Bax-dependent apoptosis.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C28 provide background on apoptotic cell death and the retinal model system, supported by citations. These establish the biological context but are not novel findings from this study.

results.result: Previous work has shown that neuronal death influences microglial properties in postnatal retina, with gene signatures similar to DAM/PAM/ATM microglia, but the extent to which phagocytosis alters microglial properties and the recognition pathways involved remain unclear.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C43 summarize prior work and knowledge gaps, supported by citations. These provide important context and motivation but are not experimental findings from this study.

results.result: Retinal microglia express chemokines Ccl3 and Ccl4 in vivo, as confirmed by in situ hybridization.
results.evaluation: Claims C61 and C169 describe validation of Ccl3 and Ccl4 expression in vivo using in situ hybridization (Figure 1—figure supplement 5). This addresses potential concerns about dissociation-induced gene expression and supports the biological relevance of the scRNAseq findings.

results.result: Specific microglial clusters express genes previously identified in other contexts, including Ccl3/Ccl4 in injury-responsive microglia and PAM, Npl in lipid-droplet microglia, and Apoc1 in MS-associated microglia, with cluster 5 sharing genes with ATM and PAM.
results.evaluation: Claims C59, C60, C63, C64, C67, C68 describe comparisons to published datasets, supported by citations. These comparisons help contextualize the findings but rely on the accuracy of the cited work.

results.result: Approximately 60% of microglia in postnatal retina survive CSF1R inhibition, a property unique compared to postnatal or adult brain, with surviving microglia showing altered gene expression that requires neuronal apoptosis.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C103 describe prior findings from the authors' previous work, supported by citations. These provide important context for the current study but are not new experimental findings.

results.result: The expansion of PLX-enriched microglia could potentially be due to further reduction of homeostatic properties with CSF1R blockade.
results.evaluation: Claim C108 is a speculation about the mechanism underlying the expansion of PLX-enriched microglia, supported by a citation but not directly tested in this study. This represents a plausible hypothesis but lacks direct experimental validation.

results.result: Neuronal cell death is a key factor driving developmental microglial diversity, with multiple states coexisting in the postnatal retina and distinct pathways mediating phagocytosis, gene expression, and survival.
results.evaluation: Claims C149-C156, C205-C206 are summary conclusions integrating multiple experimental findings. These are well-supported by the collective evidence from scRNAseq, Bax KO, PLX treatment, and receptor knockout experiments.

results.result: Remodeling microglia share genes with brain developmental microglia (ATM/PAM) and disease-associated microglia (DAM), represent a majority in postnatal retina, and may transition from homeostatic states in response to neuronal death, with phagocytosis being a major aspect of heterogeneity.
results.evaluation: Claims C157-C168 provide discussion and interpretation of the findings, supported by data and citations. The transitional model (C160) is an inference from the Bax KO data, and the speculation about distinct stages of clearance (C167) is reasonable but not directly tested.

results.result: Despite postnatal RGC death being a well-characterized model, the recognition pathways for clearance were previously undefined. CR3 and Mer are known receptors, and potential compensation by other mechanisms or cell types is likely.
results.evaluation: Claims C170-C177 provide context and discussion about the state of knowledge and potential compensatory mechanisms. The speculation about compensation (C175) is reasonable given the known biology but not directly tested.

results.result: Mer and Axl have different expression patterns and roles, with Mertk being more stable and Axl more dynamic. Loss of these receptors does not profoundly affect DAM signatures in disease models, suggesting transcriptional changes may depend on other pathways, though post-transcriptional roles are possible.
results.evaluation: Claims C178-C185 provide discussion and interpretation, supported by citations and the study's data. The speculation about post-transcriptional roles (C183) is reasonable but not tested. The inference about other pathways (C182) is well-supported by the negative results.

results.result: Adult retinal microglia can be ablated by CSF1R inhibition, but postnatal microglia expressing remodeling genes are more resistant. This resistance is induced by neuronal apoptosis and may involve survival strategies evolved for periods of elevated cell death, with CSF1R signaling also promoting homeostasis.
results.evaluation: Claims C186-C197 provide discussion and interpretation, supported by citations and the study's data. The speculation about evolved survival strategies (C192) and the nature of PLX-enriched microglia (C194, C197) are reasonable but not directly tested.

results.result: Axl has been shown to inhibit apoptosis in various cell types through diverse signaling cascades, potentially including PI3K-Akt-NfkB-Bcl2 pathway. Spp1/osteopontin, which is downregulated in Axl KO microglia, is a candidate pathway for regulating microglial survival.
results.evaluation: Claims C198-C204 provide discussion of potential mechanisms, supported by citations and the observation that Spp1 is downregulated in Axl KO (C202). The mechanistic proposals are speculative but grounded in the literature and the study's findings.

results.result: Interactions with apoptotic neurons shift microglia toward distinct remodeling states and alter microglial dependence on CSF1R through Axl, with distinct recognition receptors mediating phagocytosis versus specific microglial properties including survival.
results.evaluation: Claims C11, C51, C52 are high-level summary conclusions integrating multiple experimental findings. These are well-supported by the collective evidence from all experiments, representing the main conclusions of the study.
